nameStory: This plant earned its charming name 'elephant's-ears' from its enormous, thick leaves that really do look like the broad, rounded ears of an elephant! The leaves are so substantial and leathery that they seem almost cartoon-like in their size and texture. Some folks also call it 'pigsqueak' because the thick leaves actually make a squeaking sound when you rub them together.
description: Elephant's-ears is a low-growing perennial plant that forms clumps of impressively large, thick leaves. The heart-shaped to spoon-shaped leaves can be quite substantial, emerging from the ground in rosettes and feeling almost rubbery to the touch. In spring, clusters of small pink or white flowers appear on sturdy stalks above the foliage. This hardy plant keeps its leaves through much of the winter, making it an excellent evergreen groundcover.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Huge, heart-shaped to spoon-shaped leaves that feel thick and leathery, almost like rubber. They're glossy and substantial enough that they won't tear easily when handled.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink, rose, or white flowers clustered together on thick, reddish stalks that rise above the leaves in early spring. Each tiny flower has five petals.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low clumps or mats, rarely growing taller than 12-18 inches. Spreads slowly by underground stems to create colonies.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves make a distinctive squeaking sound when rubbed together, and feel waxy or rubbery rather than soft like most plant leaves.

habitat: In New England, elephant's-ears is almost exclusively found in cultivated gardens and landscapes, as it's not native to the region. You'll spot it in shaded to partially sunny garden beds, rock gardens, and as groundcover around homes and public plantings. It prefers moist, well-drained soil and can tolerate various soil types.

seasonality.spring: Clusters of small pink or white flowers emerge on reddish stalks, usually blooming from April to May. New leaves unfurl and look fresh and glossy.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the impressive foliage remains lush and green, providing excellent groundcover. Leaves may show some browning at edges during hot, dry spells.
seasonality.fall: Leaves often develop beautiful reddish or bronze tints, especially along the edges and undersides, adding autumn color to the garden.
seasonality.winter: Many leaves persist through winter, turning deeper red or bronze colors. The thick, leathery foliage can often be found under snow, making this an evergreen presence.

funFact: The thick leaves of elephant's-ears are so tough and waxy that in their native Siberia and Mongolia, people traditionally used them as natural sandpaper to smooth wood and even brewed the dried leaves into a tea called 'Mongolian tea' that was believed to have medicinal properties!
confusionNotes: The large, heart-shaped leaves might be confused with wild ginger or some hostas, but elephant's-ears leaves are much thicker and more rubbery feeling. Remember: if the leaf squeaks when you rub it and feels like leather, you've found elephant's-ears!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'elephant's-ears,' this plant is completely different from the tropical elephant ear plants (Alocasia and Colocasia) commonly grown as houseplants or summer annuals. Those are much larger, thinner-leaved plants in an entirely different plant family.
compareHints: Elephant's-ears is the only Bergenia species commonly found in New England gardens. Within the saxifrage family, it's easily distinguished from other members like coral bells (Heuchera) by its much larger, thicker leaves and low-growing habit. While coral bells have delicate, thin leaves, elephant's-ears leaves are substantial and leathery.
